<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research on dementia care remains largely urban-centric, with limited understanding about the lived experiences and needs of people with cognitive impairment and dementia in rural communities. This scoping review aimed to understand the care priorities, service needs, and lived experiences of rural older adults with cognitive impairment and dementia in Canada.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework, we searched CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science for journal articles published from January 2015 to January 2025. Two reviewers independently screened the articles and extracted data from the relevant articles. We used reflexive thematic analysis to analyze the data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The scoping review identified 616 initial articles, with 16 relevant studies included in our review. Four interconnected themes were identified: i) complex navigational pathways and barriers in rural dementia care; ii) limited dementia knowledge creates challenges across the disease trajectory; iii) gaps in access to dementia-related services and supports; and iv) dementia-related stigma, fear, and social isolation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings revealed critical challenges in navigating rural dementia care, where geographical distance, misinformation, limited services, and dementia-related stigma exacerbate cognitive care disparities. Addressing these challenges requires ingenuity and prioritizing lived experience research to inform community-relevant solutions. Strategic investment and implementation science are needed to co-design, implement, and evaluate navigational support models and interdisciplinary dementia care hubs to improve rural access. Advancing rural dementia care requires moving beyond documenting challenges to evaluating scalable population-level interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Understanding the Care Priorities, Service Needs, and Lived Experiences of Rural Older Adults with Dementia and Cognitive Impairment in Canada: A Scoping Review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Workplace violence (WPV) in healthcare has increased over the last decade, yet limited evidence exists to guide home health agency (HHA) prevention efforts. This study examined HHA leaders and staff WPV experiences, including the type of violence, risk factors, and prevention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted one-on-one semi-structured phone interviews with a purposive HHA sample of (a) 105 leaders, each representing a different organization, between November 2020-December 2022 and (b) 28 staff from five agencies between April 2023-August 2025. The socioecological framework guided the thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders and staff contrasted the solitary, uncontrolled, and unpredictable HHA work environment with institutional healthcare contexts. HHA staff experiences reflected three types of WPV (i.e., criminal intent, violence perpetrated by the patient or others in the home, ideological violence perpetrated by the public). WPV risk factors spanned all domains of the socioecological framework. HHA staff and leaders described individual- and organizational-level WPV prevention strategies that targeted risk factors across framework domains. There was an absence of prevention strategies initiated at the community- and societal-level (e.g., WPV prevention legislation). Organizational strategies extended beyond annual staff training to include patient-specific safety plans, employing safety escorts, and discharge protocols for patient non-compliance with safety plans.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fostering HHA staff safety within the context of service delivery is complex and multi-dimensional. Findings emphasized the importance of a comprehensive approach that is tailored to the HHA’s community and populations served and a need for societal-level policies addressing WPV prevention and mitigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Workplace Violence in Home Health: Staff and Leadership Experiences and Strategies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical exercise is widely recognized as an effective non-pharmacological intervention that improves not only functional capacity, but also cognition and quality of life in older adults. However, the molecular pathways through which it influences aging-related processes remain incompletely understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize current evidence on the effects of structured physical exercise intervention on molecular biomarkers associated with inflammation and oxidative stress in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Randomized controlled trials which included participants ≥65 years old were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 50 reports (4,379 participants) were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 38 of them in the different meta-analyses performed. Exercise interventions ranged from 8 weeks to 12 months and included aerobic, resistance, and multicomponent training. Pooled analyses indicated modest but significant reductions in C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and high-sensitivity CRP, as well as increases in IL-10. Effects on other pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and TNF-α, were inconsistent across studies. Evidence from a limited number of trials (n = 6) also suggested improvements in redox balance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, structured physical exercise demonstrates a moderate immunomodulatory and antioxidant effect in older adults, although bias was moderate to high. PROSPERO registry: CRD420251006248.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Compared to other age groups, older adults are often marginalized in the design processes of digital technologies leading to digital and social exclusion. While these aspects have been discussed in several reviews, an overarching perspective on how older adults are involved in Participatory Approaches (PA) in technology and innovation development is currently missing. This scoping review of reviews provides an overarching view on the narratives, trends, and gaps in PA in different fields of innovation, and proposes future research and practice directions. The study followed the Arksey & O’Malley’s protocol for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR checklist as the reporting guideline. Seven databases were screened for studies with a thematic focus on older adults, applying PA in technology and technology-related innovation, and published between 2014-2024. Twenty-two reviews were included. PA with older adults have seemingly evolved over the years with an increased focus on values equity, empowerment, power-sharing, and mutual learning. Nevertheless, deficit narratives on aging and ageism still constrain meaningful participation. A "participation gap" persists in which: terminology remains inconsistent; older adults are predominantly assigned roles of informants or testers rather than co-designers or equal partners; methods are mainly data-extractive; marginalized subgroups remain systematically underrepresented; and the technology scope remains predominantly care-centric. Identified gaps highlight the need for standardizing meaningful participation by creating a seal of quality for participatory approaches, improved reporting, and stronger inclusion of underrepresented populations and life domains of older persons.</jats:p>
title: Participatory Approaches with Older Adults in Technology and Innovation Research: A Scoping Review of Reviews

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An older subjective age is associated with worse cognitive health outcomes. Less is known about subjective age and cognitive function in daily life. The present study examines whether (1) baseline subjective age relates to momentary cognitive performance and nightly evaluations of subjective age and cognition, (2) daily cognitive performance relates to nightly evaluations of subjective age, and (3) nightly subjective age and cognition covary.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (N = 292, age range 40-70) reported on their subjective age at baseline, completed three cognitive tasks (Dot Memory, Symbol Search, Multiple Object Tracking) three times a day, and reported their nightly subjective age and perceived cognition for eight days.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multilevel growth models revealed that older baseline subjective age was associated with older nightly subjective age (b = 39.69, SE = 5.43, p &lt;.001), worse nightly subjective cognition (b = 24.175, SE = 5.598, p &lt;.001), and greater intraindividual variability in processing speed (b = 0.23, SE = 0.06, p &lt; .001). Additionally, nightly reports of older subjective age were associated with worse nightly subjective cognition (BP: -0.206, SE = 0.02, p &lt;.001; WP: b = -0.355, SE = 0.053, p&lt; .001). Baseline subjective age was unrelated to mean-level cognitive performance, and objective cognitive performance was unrelated to nightly subjective age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline subjective age did not relate to momentary cognitive performance, whereas both baseline levels and nightly fluctuations in subjective age were consistently linked to nightly perceptions of cognitive functioning, underscoring their relevance for understanding everyday cognitive experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Moment-to-Moment Performance and Nightly Subjective Assessments: Multi-Timescale Associations Between Subjective Age and Cognitive Function

records.abstract: <jats:p>The adoption of care robots for older adult care is often framed as a question of whether older adults will accept the technology. This paper argues that, in family-based care for older adults at home, an equally important question is how adult children position care robots within intergenerational care relationships and their responsibility for ageing parents. Using Q methodology with 42 Chinese only children, by-person factor analysis identified four profiles: the Worried Controller, who may prioritise safety over parental autonomy; the Modern Filial, who sees tailored robots as a contemporary expression of filial piety; the Presence Keeper, who resists technologies that substitute for family presence; and the Filial Complementarity Conditionalist, who sees robots as supplementary to filial and emphasises broader policy and service conditions. records.abstract: <jats:p>The use of digital tools in reminiscence interventions has increased in recent years, encompassing multimedia platforms, virtual reality (VR), digital life storybooks, and interactive applications. Yet, evidence regarding the effectiveness of digital reminiscence-based interventions remains limited. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesise the existing evidence on digital reminiscence-based interventions in care homes, with a focus on: (i) their development and evaluation; (ii) the extent to which they address cultural diversity and inclusivity; (iii) the support provided to end users; and (iv) the barriers and facilitators influencing their implementation. A systematic search of five databases (MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science), and three grey literature sources (BASE, King’s Fund Database, PsyArXiv) was undertaken. Reference lists of key papers were also hand-searched. Studies of all methodologies (qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods) were included. Sixteen studies involving 365 participants met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were grouped into: (i) digital reminiscence, (ii) digital life story, and (iii) immersive VR. Reminiscence and life story interventions improved emotional wellbeing and social engagement, while VR mainly supported stimulation and mood. Stakeholder involvement in design of technology was limited, especially for people with dementia, and reporting on cultural diversity was minimal. Variation in intervention design and outcomes limited conclusions on overall effectiveness. Implementation facilitators were ability to personalise content, care provider/home manager support, staff engagement and training, and family involvement. Barriers included technology usability, organisational infrastructure and support, workforce knowledge and capacity, and difficulties integrating into routine care practices. Digital reminiscence generally improved wellbeing, mood, cognition, communication, social interaction, although findings were mixed and limited by small samples, and varied intervention designs and outcome measures. Future research should prioritise co-creation with people with dementia, families, and staff; include more diverse populations across the disease trajectory; and explore sustainable integration into routine care practice.</jats:p>
title: Digital Reminiscence-Based Interventions to Enhance Social Interaction of People With Dementia in Care Homes: A Scoping Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>Honoring individual preferences, like going outside, can enhance the health of nursing home (NH) residents living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Although a hallmark of person-centered care, honoring ADRD residents’ preferences is often restricted when they are perceived to be high-risk for harm by NH staff. Accessible and efficient strategies are needed to help NH staff balance harmful risks to health and safety against the residents’ right to make autonomous choices, especially in under-resourced rural areas. This pilot study (NCT05618678) evaluated the feasibility of Decision-making In aGing and demeNtIa for auTonomY (DIGNITY), a multi-faceted and innovative, theory-based, person-centered risk management intervention aimed at assisting NH staff in respecting the preferences of rural residents living with ADRD, while optimizing safety. Feasibility was assessed using retention rates, staff surveys, and qualitative feedback. Fifty-two NH staff participated (88.7% female, 83.3% White, 94.3% non-Hispanic, and 48% with ≥6 years NH experience), with a 79% retention rate and 87.8% survey response rate. In the DIGNITY group, average scores (on Likert scale of 1–5) indicated high feasibility (3.99), acceptability (4.19), and appropriateness (4.24). Qualitative feedback highlighted the value of in-person training and telemonitoring sessions. The high ratings for feasibility, acceptability, and appropriateness of DIGNITY show its potential for supporting NH staff to more confidently provide person-centered care for ADRD residents.</jats:p>
title: Feasibility of the DIGNITY Intervention to Support Person-Centered Risk Management  in Rural Nursing Homes

                  <jats:p>Greater age deviation (AgeDev), in which a person’s biological age is older than their chronological age, is associated with worse cognitive performance. Most findings, however, rely on lab-administered cognitive measures and do not account for time-ordered effects of practice. The present study leveraged a measurement burst dataset to examine six distinct features of cognitive performance (peak performance, change in peak performance, intraindividual variability, forgetting, retest-related gains), and explored whether individual differences in these features can be predicted by AgeDev. In a sample of 139 adults aged 25-65, baseline AgeDev (Horvath1, Horvath2, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge), DunedinPACE, and SystemsAge were derived from DNA methylation. Across four annual high-frequency assessment bursts, processing speed and working memory were assessed via a Symbol Search and N-Back task, respectively. Using Bayesian Double Exponential Models (BDEMs), we found that baseline peak performance was lower for individuals with greater AgeDev, DunedinPACE, and chronological age. Interestingly, individuals with greater AgeDev and faster DunedinPACE showed greater retest-related gains within and across bursts. Neither AgeDev nor chronological age predicted differences in cognitive change across time. Individuals with greater AgeDev showed more intraindividual variability in processing speed. Finally, greater chronological age (but not AgeDev) was linked with more forgetting between bursts in both tasks. These findings underscore the value of multidimensional indices of cognitive performance. Importantly, even in a sample spanning young adulthood through early old age, such indices may provide unique information regarding the nature of longitudinal patterns in cognition associated with chronological or biological aging.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Frailty and cognitive decline are common among older adults, increasing risks of disability and loss of independence. We have previously demonstrated in mice that short session (≤10 minute) high-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an effective intervention for frailty, but benefits for cognitive function and reducing hallmarks of aging have not been examined. Thus, we studied 24-month-old female C57BL/6J mice from our previous study that remained sedentary or performed a 10-minute HIIT regimen 3-days-a-week for 8 weeks. We found HIIT improved cognitive aspects including an increase in T-maze alternation % and novel object recognition, but no differences were observed in Barnes maze or light-dark preference. To explore HIIT impacts on the hallmarks of aging, we examined liver, gastrocnemius muscle, and cortex brain tissues for mitochondria expression, autophagy, cellular senescence, and telomere length. HIIT increased expression of mitochondrial complexes I and V, as well as PGC1α and SIRT3 in all tissues. Autophagy marker beclin was elevated across all tissues, while p62 was increased in liver and muscle but not in the cortex, and LC3-II was lower in muscle and liver. Senescence marker p16 was lower in HIIT muscle and liver, whereas p21 decreased in liver but increased in muscle. Telomere lengths were greater in liver, but no changes in muscle or cortex. Additionally, within the group of sedentary mice, we identified differences in hallmarks of aging that potentially underlie frailty as measured using different mouse frailty assessment tools. These results highlight the potential for multi-tissue geroprotective benefits of short session HIIT to reduce frailty and improve cognition for healthy aging.</jats:p>
title: Hallmarks of Aging Associate with High Intensity Interval Training Benefits and Frailty in Female C57Bl/6J Mice

                  <jats:p>Although mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) is involved in aging and age-related neurodegenerative diseases, the impact of ALDH2 on age-related cognitive deficits and its underlying mechanisms have not been fully elucidated.                     <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In China, most people living with dementia receive care at home from family members. Dementia caregiving changes over time, yet less is known about how caregivers’ support needs are reconfigured within ongoing home-based care as family responsibilities and interactions with health and care services change. This study explored how caregivers retrospectively described changes in caregiving responsibilities and associated support needs across the home-based dementia care trajectory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative descriptive study involved 38 primary family caregivers in Guangzhou, China, who participated in face-to-face semi-structured interviews between February and December 2024. Participants were recruited using purposive maximum variation sampling, and data were analysed using the framework method. The identified phases were treated as analytically reconstructed and overlapping rather than fixed or linear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Support needs did not simply increase over time but were reconfigured as family care work changed. Before formal help-seeking, caregivers had to interpret ambiguous changes, judge whether they warranted concern, and decide how to seek help. They therefore needed accessible risk-recognition information, clear entry points to assessment, and low-barrier, non-stigmatising routes to formal support. While engaging with services, caregiving shifted towards navigating pathways, coordinating across settings, maintaining continuity, and negotiating family decisions. Caregivers consequently needed clearer care pathways, continuity and handover support, service coordination, and family decision support. While sustaining care at home, the central challenge became maintaining everyday manageability amid repetitive tasks, symptom fluctuation, emotional strain, and financial pressure. Caregivers needed practical relief, actionable symptom-management guidance, emotional support, financial protection, and services compatible with family routines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Caregivers’ support needs were shaped not only by dementia-related changes, but also by the reorganisation of family care work and encounters with fragmented services. These findings suggest that support may be more responsive when aligned with transitions in caregiving responsibilities and service engagement rather than with dementia severity alone.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>The convergence of increasing extreme heat events due to climate change and rapid population aging poses a critical public health challenge. While previous studies have identified risk factors for heat-related health outcomes, most have been conducted in Western countries and have relied on indicators that require resource-intensive surveys. This study aims to identify factors associated with heat-related illness among the elderly in Japan using practical, policy-relevant indicators.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>

Elderly residents were recruited from two distinct populations: a large public housing complex and a socially active community club. The primary outcome was the self-reported history of heat-related illness within five years, defined as episodes requiring ambulance transport or hospital visits. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors (Significance level:
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Against the backdrop of the “Dual Carbon” goals and accelerated population aging, changes in household demographic structure may influence household carbon emissions; however, existing research has not fully examined these effects and their heterogeneity at the micro household level. This study aims to investigate the impact of population aging on household carbon emissions and its heterogeneity based on Chinese household microdata.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the 2018 China General Social Survey (CGSS), this study employed the STIRPAT model and OLS regression. It characterizes population aging from three dimensions—“whether there are elderly members”, “proportion of elderly members”, and “average age of elderly members”—to examine its impact on total household carbon emissions, direct carbon emissions, and indirect carbon emissions, and further analyzes the heterogeneity of urban-rural, regional, climate conditions, as well as the mediating effect of household expenditure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study found a significant negative correlation between population aging and household carbon emissions, with the “structural effect” being stronger than the “age effect”. Households with elderly members have significantly reduced carbon emissions, and the higher the proportion of elderly members, the more significant the reduction in household carbon emissions. The impact of population aging on indirect carbon emissions is stronger than that on direct carbon emissions, indicating that it mainly exerts its effect by reducing expenditure and adjusting consumption structure. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the reduction in household carbon emissions caused by population aging is more pronounced in rural, central, and northern China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging has reduced household carbon emissions, which is of significant value for low-carbon governance. Policymakers should incorporate population aging into the household emission reduction framework and consider urban-rural and regional differences to promote differentiated low-carbon policy design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mobility is fundamental to healthy ageing and quality of life, as it enables older adults to continue participating in all spheres of life, including social, cultural, civic, spiritual, and economic activities. This study explored and compared the perspectives of Canadian and Nigerian older adults regarding life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline. The two distinct national contexts provided insight into mobility decline between high-income and low-resource settings shaped by unique cultural, economic, and policy environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We recruited eighteen Canadian and eighteen Nigerian community-dwelling older adults from diverse sociodemographic strata through community-based organisations. Using a qualitative description design, we interviewed the participants about their experiences with and observations about mobility decline. The transcripts were coded and analysed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 36 participants aged 65 to 89 years, 47.2% were women, 66.7% had a spouse or partner, and 86.1% were middle-income earners. We categorised findings into four domains: demographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural, and socioenvironmental factors. Demographic factors such as older age, ageism, women’s gender roles, and singlehood or widowhood were perceived to influence mobility decline among older adults negatively. However, most Canadian participants perceived no gender-related influence, highlighting the cultural differences in perspectives between the two groups. Socioeconomic factors (education, occupation type, and income), sociocultural factors (traditional dietary patterns, religious practices, and social participation), and socioenvironmental factors (urban versus rural living conditions, housing, and climatic challenges) were also perceived to influence the mobility trajectories of older adults. Most Canadians perceived poorer mobility among rural dwellers, while Nigerians believed the converse. We also documented the recommendations that participants made for mitigating mobility decline, including their advocacy for supportive environments and policies that recognise the unique sociodemographic contexts of older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sociodemographic factors may disproportionately influence mobility decline. Policymakers can enhance equity in ageing experiences by implementing age-friendly community initiatives that support the mobility of older adults, especially in low-resource and rural areas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>

                    <jats:p>An increase in foreign-born workers in nursing homes (NHs) has challenged first-line managers to implement language initiatives for their staff. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify three main categories and seven subcategories.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed, particularly in outpatient settings by general practitioners. In older patients with polypharmacy, inappropriate DOAC prescribing represents a major patient safety concern, potentially leading to therapeutic failure or preventable harm. To assess the quality and safety of DOAC prescriptions at hospital admission and discharge among older adults in 2023. Secondary objectives were to identify factors associated with inappropriate prescribing, characterize underlying prescribing errors, and compare these findings with data from 2018.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a prospective, observational, multicentre study across three French university hospitals, including departments of cardiology, internal medicine, post-emergency, and acute geriatrics. Older adults who were taking DOACs prior to admission and hospitalized for >24 hours were consecutively enrolled between November 2022 and May 2023. Appropriateness was defined according to European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines. Predictive factors were analyzed using logistic regression, and comparisons with 2018 data were made using χ² tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 536 eligible patients (mean age 84.1± 8.5 years; 50.6% women), 421 were included in the primary analysis. Most received apixaban (70.1%) for atrial fibrillation (83.6%). Inappropriate prescriptions were identified in 32.0% on admission and 24.9% at discharge (p = 0.004). Age >80 years (OR=1.80, CI95%= 1.20-2.72) and serum creatinine >133 µmol/L (OR=1.84, CI95%= 1.13-2.98) were associated with admission inappropriateness; age >80 years remained a discharge risk factor (OR=2.71, CI95%= 1.63-4.61), while weight <60 kg was protective (OR=0.42, CI95%= 0.25-0.69). No significant changes were observed compared to 2018.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Inappropriate DOAC prescribing during hospital transitions remains common in older adults, driven by advanced age and impaired renal function. The absence of substantial improvement since 2018 suggests that further efforts to optimize DOAC prescribing are warranted. Future interventions, including pharmacist-led medication reviews and integrated prescribing tools, could be considered to improve DOAC prescribing appropriateness in older adults.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical trial not applicable.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mealtimes in long-term care facilities are complex and serve multiple purposes. They provide opportunities for participation and learning, involving residents, relatives and healthcare professionals, each with unique circumstances. Participation and learning are central to healthy ageing. Healthcare professionals play a key role in enabling participation and learning among those involved, although these opportunities may be shaped by their perceptions and attitudes. Therefore, this study aimed to explore healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning among residents, their relatives, and colleagues related to mealtime situations in long-term care facilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews with 23 healthcare professionals (nursing assistants, licensed practical nurses, and registered nurses) working in long-term care facilities in a municipality in south-eastern Sweden. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Three themes were generated: (1)
                      <jats:italic>Shaped by relationships and circumstances</jats:italic>
                      , (2)
                      <jats:italic>Rewarding yet challenging</jats:italic>
                      , and (3)
                      <jats:italic>Prerequisites influence opportunities.</jats:italic>
                      Participation and learning related to mealtime situations manifested in various ways and to differing degrees, from extensive to almost non-existent. It was a balancing act for the healthcare professionals managing multiple challenges to enable participating and learning; however, residents and relatives were seldom invited to engage in this problem-solving. For participation and learning to occur, prerequisites were required at all levels in the organisation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare professionals perceive that participation and learning among residents, relatives, and colleagues in long-term care facilities do occur, but to varying degrees and are associated with multiple challenges. Drawing on a learning model, such as Illeris, can help identify which components need to be developed, which together with a deeper understanding and implementation of person-centredness, could contribute to increased participation and learning, and thereby to the wellbeing of residents, relatives, and healthcare professionals. However, this approach must permeate the entire organisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Incontinence is a chronic condition that affects millions of adults over the age of 65 in the United States. This study estimates the direct medical costs of incontinence for this population and identifies some possible root causes driving these costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective analysis relied on administrative claims data from the 2018 Medicare Limited Data Set. The cost analysis was limited to fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare beneficiaries over the age of 65 enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B. Our analysis of urinary tract infections (UTIs) relied on a Medicare Advantage dataset from 2016 to 2018 that included service and drug costs. We used diagnosis codes and place-of-service codes from the 2018 claims experience to identify incontinent members and their respective care setting. We used propensity score matching of incontinent and non-incontinent members to estimate the incremental cost of incontinence, controlling for age, gender, regional state groupings, and 79 comorbidities based on ICD-10CM codes, categorized into 9 disease groups. We also created an event study of UTIs to explore whether the cost of a UTI episode differs based on the presence of incontinence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On average, direct medical costs for incontinent members were $404 per member per month (PMPM) in 2018 USD higher than their non-incontinent counterparts in the same care setting. This gap rises to $968 PMPM when averaged over all members across all four care settings because it accounts for the disproportionate migration of incontinent members into more intensive and expensive care settings. A significant driver of these costs is the higher prevalence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) among incontinent members. Using an event study of UTIs, we also find that the treatment costs for UTIs are 52% higher, on average, for incontinent members.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The direct medical cost of incontinence for adults over 65 is comparable in magnitude to other major chronic conditions such as obesity, cancer, and diabetes, yet receives far less policy and management attention. Payers and institutions can make meaningful gains in reducing this cost by investing in incontinence management strategies that reduce UTIs, support caregivers, and prevent transitions to higher-intensity care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The direct medical cost of urinary and fecal incontinence by care settings for adults over 65 in the United States

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Alzheimer disease (AD) is a leading cause of dementia, and there is growing interest in scalable approaches for early screening using speech-based tasks. While prior work has demonstrated promising results using either transcript-based language features or acoustic cues, most approaches remain unimodal or rely on simple fusion strategies that do not explicitly consider interactions across modalities.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Our method uses a new bidirectional cross-attention mechanism to achieve a unified multimodal embedding for downstream tasks. We evaluate the approach on 2 tasks: AD detection by classifying whether the participant has AD or not, and AD severity assessment by predicting Mini-Mental Status Examination cognitive scores.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early mortality after long-term care facility (LTCF) admission is common; yet, prognostic tools are often derived from Western minimum dataset-based cohorts or require hospital electronic health record linkages that are unavailable at intake in many LTCFs. There is also limited evidence on explainable, admission-feasible machine learning–based prognostication in Asian LTCF settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of the study is to develop and temporally externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting 6-month all-cause mortality among older adults newly admitted to LTCFs in Taiwan using routinely collected LTCF assessment data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the JUBO Long-Term Care Database, a nationwide private administrative registry covering 636 LTCFs (37.4% of the national LTCFs) in Taiwan. We included residents with first-time LTCF admission and prespecified nonoverlapping cohorts for temporal validation: development (January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2023; n=23,901) and external validation (January 1 to December 31, 2024; n=6216). The outcome measure was death within 180 days of admission. We compared a nonlinear ensemble model (hybrid of extreme gradient boosting and random forest [HybridXGBRF]) with 7 other algorithms, including tree-based and linear benchmarks. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      ), and calibration (Brier score and calibration plots) were assessed. Model interpretability was examined using Shapley Additive Explanations.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the development cohort, 5272 of 23,901 (22.1%) residents died within 180 days. In the 2024 temporal validation cohort, 1781 of 6216 (28.7%) residents died. In internal cross-validation, HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models (0.89, 95% CI 0.88‐0.89). In temporal validation, HybridXGBRF maintained strong discrimination (AUROC 0.90, 95% CI 0.89‐0.91), with an accuracy of 0.85 and an
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.68. Calibration plots indicated close agreement between predicted and observed risks across most probability ranges, with mild divergences at higher predicted risks. Shapley Additive Explanations analysis identified frequent hospitalizations within 6 months, activities of daily living impairment, and weight loss as influential predictors. The model showed stable AUROC across sex and age strata (0.89‐0.90) and maintained high discrimination among residents with improving activities of daily living scores (AUROC 0.91, 95% CI 0.90‐0.92).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An interpretable machine learning model using routinely collected Taiwanese LTCF assessment data achieved strong discrimination, acceptable calibration, and stable temporal validation performance without requiring hospital-based electronic health record linkage. The HybridXGBRF had the highest AUROC among the evaluated models, but performance differences from extreme gradient boosting were small. The model may serve as a risk-stratification tool to help identify residents who could benefit from structured care review, advance care planning, or palliative care assessment. Prospective implementation studies could determine its impact on care processes and resident- or family-centered outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and Temporal External Validation of a Parsimonious, Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Predicting 6-Month Mortality in Long-Term Care Facilities: A Retrospective Cohort Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.28;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), mean intrinsic motivation increased from 5.94 (SD 1.00) to 6.29 (SD 0.81; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.40;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and mean habit strength increased from 3.34 (SD 1.11) to 3.81 (SD 0.84; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.42;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). In adjusted mixed models, habit strength remained higher at T2 than at baseline (β=0.362, 95% CI .113-.611;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and at T2 (β=7.390, 95% CI 5.370-9.410;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) than at baseline. Among the COM-B domains, only opportunity was associated with greater immediate posttraining physical activity improvement (time × opportunity interaction β=26.464, 95% CI 3.191-49.737;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Existing home-based fall prevention strategies often adopt a one-size-fits-all approach despite substantial heterogeneity among older adults with stroke. Persona-based methods may facilitate more individualized intervention design, yet remain largely unexplored in stroke rehabilitation. This study explored variations in fall prevention self-management among older adults with stroke and developed user personas to represent their diverse experiences, challenges, and support needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative descriptive study was conducted among 26 older adults with stroke receiving home-based care in China. Participants were recruited using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and March 2026. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify key dimensions of fall prevention self-management. Individual participant profiles were iteratively synthesized through cross-case comparison into composite personas representing recurring configurations of behaviors, beliefs, barriers, resources, and support needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five distinct personas emerged: proactive self-managers, risk-discounting managers, routine-based managers, support-constrained managers, and professionally supported managers. These personas demonstrated distinct combinations of fall-risk perception, social resources, environmental constraints, and healthcare dependence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings demonstrate substantial diversity in how older adults with stroke manage fall prevention in home settings. Persona-based stratification provides an actionable approach for designing scalable, context-sensitive fall prevention interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Tailored personas for home-based fall prevention among older adults with stroke: A qualitative study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory study examines changes in depressive symptoms following spousal loss relative to remaining married across countries, whether these associations vary by national context and gender, and the extent to which selection into widowhood accounts for cross-national differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study uses data from the Health and Retirement Study international family of studies and evaluates change in depressive symptoms across six country contexts: United States, England, Mexico, China, and two combinations of European Union countries categorized by welfare state: Conservative and Social/Democratic. We evaluated change in depressive symptoms among individuals who were married at Wave 1 (2015/2016 depending on country) and at Wave 2 (2018) when some remained married while others reported a spousal loss. The analytic sample included adults aged 60 years and older (Wave 1 mean age = 69.13 years, standard deviation [SD] = 6.78).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using ordinary least squares regression and propensity score methods to account for selection into widowhood, results suggest that the experience of widowhood is generally similar across country contexts, with widows experiencing, on average, about 0.5 SDs increase in depressive symptoms (marginal effect = 0.53, p &lt; .001; propensity adjusted score = 0.56, p &lt; .001), a likely clinically relevant increase, accounting for selection. These effects were roughly the same for men and women in all country contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research is needed to identify factors that may buffer the consequences of widowhood and explore university and cross-national interventions that may help reduce these effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults often face significant barriers to mental health help-seeking. This study integrated participatory co-design with behavioural science principles to develop culturally meaningful hybrid nudges to normalise mental health help-seeking among older adults in Hong Kong.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve older adults with mental health volunteering experience participated in eight researcher-facilitated co-design workshops structured by design thinking principles. A graphic designer assisted in visualising the prototypes. Workshop artefacts, design outputs, structured summaries, and focus group recordings were analysed using thematic analysis. The study was primarily an intervention development study; focus group data were used as an embedded process evaluation to understand participants’ experiences of co-design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Co-designers were 75% female with a mean age of 63.83 years. The co-design process produced a set of hybrid nudge prototypes with two design orientations: (1) reminiscence-oriented using metaphors from childhood games to cue autonomy and peer support, and (2) psychoeducation-oriented using relatable vignettes to model perspective taking. Although the project initially aimed to create social norms and visual nudges, co-designers preferred integrating brief psychoeducational and general well-being content to increase acceptability. The embedded process evaluation highlighted perceived learning, ownership, and collaboration, as well as challenges such as self-doubt.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participatory co-design can support the development of theory-informed and culturally attuned hybrid nudges to address motivational barriers to mental health help-seeking. Future research should test acceptability and behavioural outcomes through randomized or pragmatic trials, and examine how to balance theoretical fidelity with participant agency in co-designed behavioural interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Developing hybrid nudges to promote mental health help-seeking in Chinese older adults: A co-design approach

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families’ and staff’s acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants’ narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Families and frontline staff should not be considered merely as end users, but as key stakeholders whose needs and expertise should shape the direction of AI applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Is there a role for artificial intelligence in end-of-life care for persons with dementia? Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of vision impairment continues to increase globally due to population growth and aging. Among older adults with vision impairment, loneliness is common. Prior studies assessing loneliness risk have relied on regression-based approaches, which may not capture complex, heterogeneous conditional pathways. We apply a theoretically guided machine learning approach to examine loneliness risk among older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using baseline data from 210 adults with AMD (Agemean = 80.1 years) enrolled in a randomized controlled trial, we applied a decision tree method using measures of legal blindness, emotional responses to vision loss, social life satisfaction, anxiety, depression, optimism, future planning, and sociodemographic factors to investigate heterogeneous pathways to loneliness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Decision tree models demonstrated stable discrimination (AUCtrain=.88, AUCtest=.78, DeLong 95% CI: 0.68–0.88) and robust classification performance across thresholds. Social life satisfaction emerged as the primary branching condition differentiating loneliness outcomes. Distinct pathways suggested that high social life satisfaction was strongly associated with lower loneliness; optimism served as a compensatory resource when social satisfaction was lower. Additional pathways highlighted the effects of vision loss severity, anxiety, and emotional responses to vision loss on loneliness. Depressive symptoms differentiated loneliness outcomes within a lower-anxiety branch, suggesting depression may overshadow protective factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that loneliness arises through heterogeneous psychological pathways rather than single risk factors. By identifying conditional configurations of psychosocial and health-related factors, interpretable decision-tree models may inform more targeted screening, evaluation, and intervention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Conditional pathways to loneliness in older adults with vision impairment: A decision-tree analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Financial abuse is a prevalent yet underreported form of elder abuse with serious health and economic consequences. Prior research has linked poor relationship quality to financial abuse risk, but most studies rely on cross-sectional designs and focus on a single relationship type. This study examined whether 10-year changes in relationship quality with spouses, family, and friends are associated with subsequent financial abuse.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by social exchange theory, this study used data from three waves of the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project. Relationship quality was categorized as stable, improving, or worsening over a 10-year period. Logistic regression models were estimated for each relationship type, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with worsening family or friendship relationships over the 10-year period had more than twice the odds of experiencing subsequent financial abuse compared with those with stable relationships. Improving relationship trajectories were not significantly associated with financial abuse risk. Changes in spousal relationship quality were also not significantly associated with financial abuse.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that worsening family and friendship relationships over time may be an early indicator of financial abuse risk. Monitoring changes in older adults’ social relationships and supporting relationship stability may be important strategies for preventing financial abuse in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Relationship Quality Trajectories and Financial Abuse Among Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Resident-to-resident aggression (RRA) is the most common form of elder mistreatment in long-term care settings. Although race/ethnicity is likely a contributing factor, research has been limited in examining the role of residents’ race and ethnicity in RRA. We sought to define and qualitatively examine the predisposing factors and acute precipitants of race/ethnicity-related resident-to-resident aggression (RE-RRA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the socioecological model, events-based perspective, and conceptual work on stigma-based aggression, we developed qualitative interview and data analytical guides. We conducted nine focus groups and twelve in-depth interviews with 81 nursing home staff from multiple clinical and non-clinical roles across two long-term care facilities on the U.S. East Coast. We coded qualitative data using a deductive thematic qualitative approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA appeared to be a recurring interpersonal dynamic, though its full scope is likely under-detected and under-recognized. We identified five major types of RE-RRA, including physical violence, microaggression, social exclusion, and avoidance. Ten predisposing factors and eight acute precipitants uniquely contributed to RE-RRA, highlighting the importance of considering distinct race- and ethnicity-related elements in prevention research. We summarized our findings in a conceptual framework for RE-RRA that may be useful for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA is a distinct phenomenon shaped by identifiable predisposing and precipitating factors, offering opportunities for future prevention and intervention development. These findings underscore the importance of integrating RE-RRA within staff education, existing clinical governance structures, including incident reporting, and quality improvement processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Exploring the Role of Race and Ethnicity in Resident-to-Resident Aggression: A Qualitative Study

                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Palliative care (PC) consultation outcomes in nursing homes (NHs) are often assessed using health systems' clinical and utilization metrics rather than outcomes from the perspective of the key partners who provide and sustain it. This study was designed to identify meaningful PC consultation outcomes from the perspectives of NH staff, PC consultants, and NH/PC agency directors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the team conducted semi-structured interviews with key partners from 14 NHs in the Eastern United States. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (N = 33) included NH staff (e.g., primary care providers and nurses), PC consultants (e.g., PC physicians and PC nurse practitioners), and leaders (e.g., NH directors and PC agency directors). Key partners reported meaningful outcomes in four domains: resident, family, NH staff, and NH facility. Resident outcomes included goal-concordant care, symptom management, hospitalization rates, and understanding of care choices and control. Family outcomes included shared decision-making, understanding of the resident’s disease trajectory and management measures, and feeling supported. NH staff outcomes included capacity to provide high-quality care and emotional support. Lastly, NH facility outcomes included filling care gaps, facility reputation, and organizational morale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight multi-domain and interdependent PC consultation outcomes across residents, families, staff, and NH facilities that may be overlooked in existing evaluation frameworks. Future interventions and quality measures should incorporate these outcomes and ensure that residents’ and families’ perspectives are represented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.</jats:p>
title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This manuscript analyzes the literary, social and cultural representations of dementia in Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019). I contend that the authors’ accounts of their mothers’ struggle with dementia, from its onset to its end, function as living archives of personal and national history. I employ life writing, aging studies, and, to a lesser extent, historiography to examine the literary, social cultural, and historical dimensions of such experiences. I address the narrative construction of the mothers’ identity in later life by highlighting the role of archives and family memories in the context of contemporary South Africa. Thus, I aim to illustrate the instrumental role of life narratives in the creation of safe spaces for intergenerational dialogue and reconciliation with a troubled past on a personal and national level. I also contend that humanities-based inquiry brings to the fore the essential aspects of later life, thereby challenging the pathologizing medical in the representation of dementia, which often disregards the reality of old people as vessels of knowledge. Eventually, I showcase that illness life narratives function as accessible repositories of public knowledge that render visible the realities of aging.</jats:p>
title: Living History, Fading Minds: Dementia as the Gateway to Historical Past in South Africa via Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019)

                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hospital-to-home transitions constitute vulnerable periods during which health systems increasingly rely on unpaid care partners to help care recipients execute discharge plans. We examine how mutuality and incongruence within care partner-care recipient dyads may shape discharge preparedness and dyadic self-efficacy during care transitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a secondary qualitative analysis of PROJECT ACHIEVE focus groups and key informant interviews with 248 participants (138 care recipients, 110 care partners) across six U.S. health systems, examining their experiences of hospital-to-home transitions. A multidisciplinary team conducted thematic analysis and compared themes across stakeholder groups, guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Interdependence Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Care recipients and care partners shared goals but often differed in their appraisals of discharge readiness and post-discharge roles. Three domains of incongruence emerged: (1) preparedness for transitions home, as care recipients prioritized going home despite ongoing symptoms while care partners worried about premature discharge and inadequate training; (2) burdensomeness and struggle for independence, as care recipients desired to preserve autonomy while care partners absorbed the emotional and practical strain of supporting such desires; and (3) role changes and evolving relational identities, as spouses and adult children assumed caregiving roles that disrupted prior identities in the relationship. Lower mutuality was linked to reduced dyadic self-efficacy and, consequently, increased risk of readmission.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight dyadic incongruence as a target for intervention in care transitions. Care strategies that assess care recipient-care partner mutuality may enhance dyadic self-efficacy and improve post-discharge outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
