<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atypical survey response patterns, such as inconsistent or implausible responses, have been linked to lower cognitive functioning in later life. This study examined whether these behaviors predict future dementia onset across diverse longitudinal studies of aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a coordinated analysis of data from eight longitudinal studies of aging (total N = 76,350). We derived five common types of atypical response pattern indicators from participants’ questionnaire data. Associations with subsequent dementia risk were examined within each cohort using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic covariates and accounting for death as a competing risk. Results were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis methods.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across cohorts, significant associations with incident dementia were observed for item-nonresponse (overall hazard ratio [HR] per SD increase = 1.06), random response errors (HR = 1.25), multivariate outlier responses (HR = 1.31), and incompatible response patterns indexed by Guttman errors and person-fit statistics (HRs = 1.22–1.25). Extreme responding was not significantly associated with dementia risk. Secondary analyses suggested stronger associations among individuals younger than 75 years and those with higher levels of education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Routine survey responses contain behavioral signals associated with emerging dementia risk. Because these indicators can be derived from existing survey data without additional testing burden, they may provide a scalable complement to traditional approaches for studying cognitive aging in large population-based cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Atypical survey response patterns as early indicators of dementia onset: A coordinated analysis across longitudinal aging cohorts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sociological theory posits that social networks function as enduring relational structures that constrain and enable everyday social interactions, yet empirical evidence linking network properties to real-time social exposures remains limited. To address this gap, this study examines how older adults' social networks are associated with their daily social experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas (SECHURA) study, we combine egocentric network data (1,474 alters from 254 respondents) with ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data capturing real-time social interactions over one week (5,342 observations). We evaluate associations between three network properties–structure (quantity, composition, and interconnectedness of network members), heterogeneity (diversity in gender, race/ethnicity, and age), and strength (strong and supportive ties) – and four momentary outcomes (number and type of interaction partners, social activities, and being outside the home).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Random-effects models show that larger and more socially diverse networks are associated with greater momentary social engagement, including more interaction partners, less time alone, and more explicit socializing. Both role diversity and network density are associated with heightened social exposure, through distinct pathways. Sociodemographic heterogeneity also predicts interaction patterns, with age heterogeneity linked to kin-centered interactions and racial heterogeneity to non-kin exposure. Stronger affective ties predicted less engagement in explicit socializing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Personal social networks operate as critical structures linked to the quantity, composition, and context of older adults' real-time social exposures. Large, densely connected, and role-diverse networks appear to facilitate everyday interactions through different mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations between social network characteristics and daily social experiences in later life: Evidence from ecological momentary assessment

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D).                     <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was no significant relationship between respondents’ gender and total CSI-D reports in either country. Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place.                   </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines differences in the composition and size of the close social network among older adults in same-sex and different-sex coresidential unions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using pooled, probability-based, cross-sectional data from the 2006–2022 Health and Retirement Study, weighted fractional probit and negative binomial regression models were estimated to examine differences in close network composition (proportions of close children, immediate family members, and friends) and network size (number of close ties).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with older adults in different-sex unions, those in same-sex unions reported a higher proportion of friends and a lower proportion of children and immediate family members in their close network, though overall network size was comparable. Supplemental analyses suggested heterogeneity in these patterns. The same-sex versus different-sex gap in friend composition was larger among males than females and was similarly larger among those who were cohabiting than married. Finally, in terms of network size, males in same-sex couples reported smaller close networks than males in different-sex couples, whereas network size was equivalent between females in same-sex and different-sex couples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Beyond their partners, older adults in same-sex unions cultivate distinctly friend-centered close networks. This pattern reflects a history of intentionally built chosen ties that queers dominant assumptions about who partnered older adults designate as close. These findings affirm the importance of policies and practices that acknowledge diverse family arrangements, particularly those rooted in chosen kinship, as a fundamental step toward achieving social equity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Composition and size of close social networks among older adults in same-sex and different-sex couples

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal methods, we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences; objective physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both objective metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Positive social connections are key ingredients for healthy aging.                   <jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>To explore shared agreement on experiences of love, we surveyed a representative sample (N=400) of adults aged 65 years and older in the United States. They evaluated 61 experiences to determine whether older adults believe they typically evoke feelings of love in most people. We used a Bayesian decision tree model to account for individual differences in respondents’ knowledge and decision-making styles when deriving the consensus on these experiences.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found a consensus among older adults on experiences of love. In addition, individual differences in knowledge on love and decision-making styles were meaningfully linked to person-level characteristics: female participants and those with higher levels of compassion had higher levels of knowledge on the consensus, White male participants and those with higher levels of loneliness were more likely to guess the shared agreement when they were uncertain, and non-White participants were more likely to guess “True.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Experiences of love for older adults include both romantic and non-romantic settings. Older adults tended to have different knowledge levels regarding the consensus on these experiences. Future research could examine whether fostering compassion or raising awareness about these loving experiences in daily life might improve well-being for older adults. Increased knowledge regarding these experiences may decrease misunderstandings or loneliness by sharing more loving experiences with others.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

records.abstract: <jats:p>A sense of purpose is a central component of mental well-being in older adulthood. Although many predictors of purpose have been identified, most studies have considered a limited set, leaving their relative importance unclear. The present study addressed this gap by examining a large set of psychological, social, and demographic variables in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults from the Health and Retirement Study. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) was used to evaluate 47 predictors. Self-esteem emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by positive affect. records.abstract: <jats:p>Older adults and people of color have been disproportionately impacted by extreme weather events. We examined the moderating role of race-ethnicity in the association between age and exposure to three weather events. Three separate logistic regression models analyzed whether the relationship between age group and weather event exposures (heat wave, wildfire, or flood/intense storm) varied by race-ethnicity (White, Black, Hispanic, or Asian). Flood/intense storm exposure significantly decreased in older ages for White adults, but increased in older ages for Asian adults. records.abstract: <jats:p>Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.</jats:p>
title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>Dementia-friendly videos are adapted audiovisual resources designed to support care for people living with moderate to severe dementia. Although evidence suggests these videos can enhance comfort, engagement, and communication, little is known about how frontline healthcare providers integrate them into everyday practice. This qualitative implementation study examined the barriers and facilitators experienced by frontline healthcare providers when implementing dementia-friendly videos in real-world clinical environments. The videos were introduced over an 18-month period in two contrasting care settings in Vancouver, Canada: an acute hospital geriatric unit and a long-term care dementia unit. Nineteen interdisciplinary healthcare providers, including nurses, care aides, and rehabilitation and recreation staff, participated in semi-structured interviews and focus groups after using the videos in routine care. A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted, followed by a later-stage comparison with relevant constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A participatory research team, including people living with dementia and family caregivers, contributed to study design, interpretation, and theme refinement. Findings showed that time pressures and staffing constraints limited workflow compatibility, particularly because many residents required assistance to operate devices. Limited equipment and unstable internet access further hindered consistent use. Facilitators included motivated staff who acted as catalysts for adoption, the perceived advantages of dementia-friendly videos over general platforms, and staff observations of positive impacts on emotional regulation and participation. Seeing benefits in practice, such as calming distressed patients, reinforced continued use. The study highlights the importance of integrating dementia-friendly videos into existing workflows rather than treating them as additional tasks. Ensuring adequate equipment, supporting motivated staff, and attending to cultural and linguistic relevance are essential for sustainable implementation. These findings offer practical guidance for embedding person-centred digital tools into dementia care.</jats:p>
title: Implementing Dementia-Friendly Videos in Everyday Care: A Qualitative Study of Frontline Staff Experiences

records.abstract: <jats:p>Placement of a relative with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) in residential care is often assumed to reduce caregiver burden. However, little is known about how informal caregivers experience their role after placement. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of 9 informal family caregivers whose relatives with ADRD resided in residential care settings. Semi-structured interviews lasting 60 to 120 minutes were conducted and analyzed using Colaizzi’s method to identify the essential structures of post-placement caregiving. Brief quantitative measures, including the CES-D-10 and the Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, were collected to contextualize participants’ emotional burden. Six themes emerged: emotional dissonance after placement, cognitive load and decision fatigue, persistence of caregiver identity and responsibility, fragmented systems and resource gaps, crisis-driven transitions, and the need for post-placement support. Participants described caregiving after placement not as an endpoint, but as a reconfigured role marked by ongoing emotional labor, vigilance, advocacy, and decision-making. Although physical caregiving tasks had shifted to staff, caregivers remained deeply involved in monitoring care quality, managing communication, responding to crises, and serving as the primary emotional anchor for their relatives. Quantitative findings reinforced these accounts, with all participants scoring above the CES-D-10 clinical threshold and reporting substantial caregiver distress. Taken together, the findings suggest that caregiving continues in sustained and multidimensional ways after residential placement. Residential care settings should recognize family caregivers as ongoing partners and provide structured orientation, clearer communication pathways, and psychosocial support to address the emotional, cognitive, and relational demands of post-placement caregiving.</jats:p>
title: Continuing the Role: Lived Experiences of Family Caregivers after Placement of a Relative With Dementia in Residential Care

records.abstract: <jats:p>Care home managers’ leadership is widely recognised as shaping how staff provide care for people living with dementia. However, evidence remains limited on what enables managers to enact this role and sustain person-centred approaches within day-to-day care. This study explored managers and staffs’ experiences of facilitating person-centred care using an interpretative phenomenological approach. Twenty participants (ten managers and ten staff) from ten care homes took part in online semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using Colaizzi’s seven-step method. Participants viewed managers as key enablers of person-centred care, yet described this role as constrained and not always achievable in practice. Organisational and regulatory demands such as staffing shortages, administrative burden, and limited autonomy were perceived as major barriers, shaping what staff and managers felt able to prioritise. Managers countered these pressures, by being visible and available to staff, encouraging open communication, using staff meetings and appraisals to address concerns, and supporting staff reporting of poor practice. Values-based recruitment, emphasising empathy and kindness over formal qualifications, were also described as central to sustaining person-centred practice. However, staff were often unaware of these leadership strategies, which were frequently experienced as workarounds rather than embedded organisational processes. Examples of person-centred care focused on supporting residents’ choices in everyday routines and taking additional steps to understand individuals’ backgrounds when information was limited. Peer learning groups were valued for reducing managerial isolation and promoting shared problem-solving, whereas online and mandatory training were widely seen as insufficient. Findings highlight a persistent tension between managers and staff aspirations for person-centred care and the realities of practice shaped by system pressures, risk management, and resource constraints. Sustaining culture change requires long term organisational commitment, context sensitive leadership development, and structural support that extends beyond individual managers’ efforts.</jats:p>
title: Navigating Leadership Challenges: Care Home Managers' and their Staffs’ Experiences of Enabling Person-Centred Dementia Care, A Qualitative Study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging is leading to increased demand for health and long-term care. AI-based assistive technologies have been developed to support autonomy and care for older adults, yet real‑world adoption remains limited. We review evidence on acceptance and determinants of acceptance of AI‑based assistive technologies among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a scoping review using the JBI methodology and followed PRISMA‑ScR guidelines for reporting. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane) were searched for studies published from January 2010 to June 2025, initially in any language. We included studies examining acceptance and determinants of acceptance of AI-based assistive technologies among adults aged 65 years and older. We synthesized data using inductive thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty‑nine studies met the inclusion criteria, with over one-third conducted in Europe (n = 10). Overall attitudes toward AI‑based assistive technologies were generally favorable when technologies were perceived as useful, easy to use, and tailored to needs. However, actual use was low. Acceptance was associated with socio‑demographic (e.g., age, residence), medical (e.g., frailty, self‑rated health), psychosocial (e.g., stigma), and structural (e.g., cost, accessibility) determinants, as well as with institutional and relational factors (e.g., preservation of human contact).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While older adults have generally positive views of AI‑based assistive technologies, adoption is slow because of intersecting psychosocial, economic, technical, and organizational barriers. User‑centered design, care-led innovation approaches, and implementation strategies that complement—rather than replace—human support may facilitate uptake and sustained use. Development of standardized assessment tools is needed to enable cross-study comparability and guide future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Acceptance of AI-Based Assistive Technologies for Autonomy Support Among Older Adults: A Scoping Review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse (CCW) algorithms are widely used to identify chronic conditions in Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) claims. However, their validity in Medicare Advantage (MA) encounters remains uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a cross-sectional study using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare data. We analyzed NHATS Rounds 9 and 11, aged≥65 years, with continuous 24-month enrollment in MA or FFS. CCW algorithms were applied to identify six conditions: arthritis, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, and osteoporosis. Self-reported, physician-diagnosed conditions from NHATS interviews served as the reference standard. Survey-weighted sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and balanced accuracy were compared between MA and FFS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We included 1,708 MA and 2,239 FFS beneficiaries in Round 9 and 1,472 MA and 1,566 FFS beneficiaries in Round 11. Across both rounds, balanced accuracy was similar between MA and FFS for all six conditions. Diabetes and hypertension demonstrated high sensitivity (0.88–0.94), while arthritis and osteoporosis showed lower sensitivity but high specificity. Although statistically significant MA–FFS differences were observed for select metrics (diabetes PPV in Round 9; chronic lung disease specificity in Round 11), absolute differences were minor and not clinically meaningful.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CCW algorithms perform comparably in MA and FFS Medicare data. These findings support the validity of using CCW algorithms in MA encounter data for epidemiologic research for risk adjustment, facilitating more generalizable studies of the growing MA population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Chronic Conditions Data Warehouse Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-For-Service Populations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence comparing the performance of claims-based dementia algorithms across Medicare Advantage (MA) and fee-for-service (FFS) populations remains limited. We evaluated the validity of two claims-based algorithms across MA and FFS populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used nationally representative, linked National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS)-Medicare data to identify community-dwelling participants with continuous enrollment in MA or FFS during Round 7 (2017; n = 5,018), Round 9 (2019; n = 4,018), and Round 11 (2021-2022; n = 3,086). Using NHATS probable dementia as reference standard, we validated the Bynum-Standard and Chronic Condition Warehouse (CCW) dementia algorithms across three time points.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, both algorithms demonstrated comparable performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity (&gt;97.9%) and negative predictive value [NPV] (&gt;92.9%). The Bynum algorithm showed similar sensitivity between MA and FFS in Rounds 7 (30.2% vs. 29.1%) and 11 (25.6% vs. 23.9%), but lower sensitivity in MA for Round 9 (25.0% vs. 36.4%). Positive predictive value [PPV] was similar between MA (62.7%-70.6%) and FFS (62.1%-70.4%) across all rounds. The CCW algorithm demonstrated greater MA-FFS differences, with lower sensitivity in MA for Rounds 9 (30.8% vs. 46.9%) and 11 (35.0% vs. 49.3%) and similar sensitivity for Round 7 (40.4% vs. 42.2%). PPV varied across rounds in both MA and FFS [(Round 7: 76.3% vs. 71.2%) to (Round 11: 68.5% vs. 76.4%)]. Both algorithms identified participants with more severe dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Claims-based dementia algorithms demonstrate broadly consistent performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity and moderate PPV but comparable or lower sensitivity in MA, informing case ascertainment across Medicare plan type.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Claims-based Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite growing enrollment in Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, the performance of claims-based frailty algorithms, which were developed for Medicare fee-for-service (FFS), remains unclear in MA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We calculated the Kim claims-based frailty index (CFI), Veterans Affairs-Frailty Index (VA-FI), and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) using the National Health and Aging Trends Study linked to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) and MA data. We evaluated their performance against the comprehensive geriatric assessment-based frailty index (CGA-FI) and the frailty phenotype (FP) in Round 11 and Round 9.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 1,527 FFS and 1,457 MA beneficiaries in Round 11, frailty prevalence was 34.2% and 35.5%, respectively, by CGA-FI ≥0.25, and 13.3% and 16.2%, respectively, by FP. Across FFS and MA populations, the CFI, which prioritizes specificity and positive predictive value, classified 10-12% of the overall population and 30-36% of those with prior hospitalization as frail, whereas the VA-FI and HFRS, which emphasize sensitivity, classified 53-71% of the overall population and 56-87% of those with prior hospitalization as frail. Although claims-based frailty measures performed similarly across FFS and MA populations, their discriminatory ability was higher for CGA-FI ≥0.25 (C-statistics: CFI, 0.79-0.82; VA-FI, 0.77-0.82; HFRS, 0.63-0.77) than for FP (CFI, 0.71-0.77; VA-FI, 0.67-0.75; HFRS, 0.60-0.74). Performance was consistent by race and survey rounds, with modestly better discrimination in women than men.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Claims-based frailty measures are scalable tools for contemporary FFS and MA populations. However applying published thresholds led to differences in frailty prevalence and model performances. Thresholds should therefore be tailored to the intended.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Performance of Claims-based Frailty Indices in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sleep duration has well-established U-shaped associations with cognitive health, but research has largely ignored spousal interdependence. This study examined actor and partner effects of sleep duration on global cognition in middle-aged and older Chinese couples, testing whether associations differed by sex.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from CHARLS waves 1-4 (2011-2018). The analytical sample comprised 4,260 couples (8,520 individuals) aged ≥45 years living a married, two-person, mixed-sex household. Global cognition was assessed with a composite battery adapted from the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status and Chinese Mini-Mental State Examination; nocturnal sleep and napping durations were self-reported. Actor-Partner Interdependence Models with quadratic terms examined actor effects (own sleep predicting own cognition) and partner effects (own sleep predicting spouse’s cognition), with false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted q-values and sex-equality tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Significant inverted U-shaped actor effects were found for wives (β=-0.010, 95% CI: -0.014, -0.005, p &lt; 0.001) and husbands (β=-0.011, 95% CI: -0.016, -0.006, p &lt; 0.001); both survived FDR correction (q = 0.002, q &lt; 0.001). Husbands’ sleep was nominally associated with wives’ cognition similarly (β=-0.005, p = 0.025), while wives’ sleep was not associated with husbands’ cognition (p = 0.618). The husband-to-wife association did not survive FDR correction (q = 0.239), and sex-equality tests were non-significant (χ²(9)=9.35, p = 0.406). Napping showed limited, largely non-significant associations with cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Own nocturnal sleep duration shows a robust, symmetric inverted U-shaped association with cognitive function in both spouses. The possible husband-to-wife partner effect did not survive correction for multiple testing and warrants adequately powered investigation before informing couple-based clinical recommendations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Wife-Husband Differences in the Associations Between Sleep Durations and Global Cognition Among Middle-Aged and Older Married Couples in China: A Longitudinal Dyadic Analysis

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study examined how social disconnection, neighborhood contexts, and cognitive function trajectories are jointly and interactively associated among middle-aged and older Black adults.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>

Social disconnectedness was measured by three types of social isolation (from extended family, adult children, and friends) and loneliness (UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale). Neighborhood contextual factors included neighborhood social cohesion and physical disadvantage. Covariables included age, sex, education, marital status, and living arrangements. We used group-based trajectory modeling to test the study objectives.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified four global cognitive function trajectories: low and declining (14% of sample), moderate and declining (29%), moderate and stable (40%), and high and stable (17%). Multivariable models indicated that neighborhood physical disadvantage (RRR=.61, 95%CI[0.40, 0.92]) and social cohesion (RRR=.42, 95%CI[0.23, .77]) moderated the association between social isolation from extended family and global cognitive function trajectory membership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study is among the first to examine cognitive function trajectories with linkages to social disconnectedness and neighborhood contexts among middle-aged and older Black adults. Overall, the results suggest that neighborhood contexts condition how social isolation relates to cognitive trajectories. These findings underscore the importance of considering both social disconnectedness and neighborhood context in explaining heterogeneity in cognitive aging among middle-aged and older Black adults.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>BACKGROUND</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Human aging does not follow a single trajectory. Epigenetic changes offer insight into the heterogeneity in aging by reflecting the combined influence of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors on the timing and progression of age-related changes beyond what chronological age alone can explain. Recent studies in cancer and aging underscore the importance of methylation variability as a marker of biological dysregulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>METHODS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We investigated the role of DNA methylation in aging heterogeneity by performing epigenome-wide differential methylation and variance association analyses in blood samples from 1,445 Canadians aged 45 to 85 from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>RESULTS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified 448 differentially methylated regions and 488 differentially variable regions associated with health decline as measured by the health deficit accumulation Frailty Index, cognitive function, and physical function. These two classes of regions showed minimal overlap, with distinct gene coverage, suggesting that variability contributes a complementary signal to aging heterogeneity. Genes overlapped by differentially methylated regions were enriched for immune and inflammation-related pathways, whereas differentially variable regions highlighted additional localized, CpG‑island–enriched signals shared across health domains, consistent with regionally structured rather than diffuse dysregulation. By integrating significant CpGs from both analyses, we constructed an epigenetic biomarker. The biomarker was associated with all-cause mortality and showed higher discrimination than biomarkers constructed from differential methylation or variability alone, with a similar pattern reproduced in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>CONCLUSIONS</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that DNA methylation variability may provide a complementary dimension of epigenetic aging and support further evaluation in larger cohorts with more mortality events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Little is known about long-term risks of hospitalizations among heart failure (HF) older adults at a national level. We identified long-term patterns of hospitalizations following the diagnosis of HF and assessed whether high-risk patients can be identified prior to discharge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a retrospective cohort study from 2010 to 2020. Fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF during an inpatient stay and followed for up to 5 years. Group-based trajectory models (GBTM) identified 4 trajectories of all-cause hospitalizations during follow-up.                     <jats:p>Of the 84,597 Medicare beneficiaries with newly-diagnosed HF (mean age: 77.4 [± 7.1] years and 58.3% male), we identified 4 distinct trajectories of hospitalizations: Group 1 (n = 19,340; 22.9%) had consistently “low risks” of hospitalization, Group 2 (n = 53,922; 57.9%) had elevated risks shortly after discharge (“high-to-low risk”), Group 3 (n = 5,035; 9.8%) had elevated risks at later stages of illness (“low-to-high risk”), and Group 4 (n = 6,300; 9.4%) had consistently “high risks” of hospitalization.                   </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-risk HF patients could be identified at the time-of-diagnosis using routinely available clinical characteristics, enabling targeted interventions during critical periods to improve long-term outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is accompanied by changes in body composition and cognition. Although adiposity has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and dementia risk, associations with specific cognitive domains in later life remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study examined associations between adiposity and cognitive performance in 769 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (70–94 years) from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA). Adiposity was assessed using anthropometric measures (body mass index, waist circumference) and MRI-derived regional fat volumes, including visceral and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a screening measure (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding Test), executive function (Trail Making Test B), and memory (California Verbal Learning Test–II Short Form). Multivariable linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for demographic, cardiometabolic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater age was associated with lower adiposity and poorer cognitive performance (p &lt; 0.05). Most adiposity measures were inversely associated with processing speed after adjustment for age, sex, race, and testing site (p &lt; 0.05). These associations generally persisted after adjustment for cardiometabolic conditions and were attenuated after inclusion of education, depressive symptoms, and behavioral covariates. No significant associations were observed between adiposity and executive function. Memory outcomes showed modest, exploratory associations with abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue measures only in fully adjusted models (p = 0.03–0.07).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In healthy older adults, adiposity is most consistently related to processing speed, whereas associations with memory and executive function are weaker or absent. Processing speed may be especially sensitive to adiposity-related differences. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adiposity and Cognitive Performance in Older Men and Women from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is the strongest risk factor for most chronic diseases, yet aging-related diseases (ARDs) lack consistent, data-driven definitions. Prior work has proposed frameworks to classify ARDs based on age-specific onset patterns, but applications have largely relied on demographically homogeneous populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We extended a data-driven framework integrating unsupervised clustering and actuarial modeling to electronic health record data from 633,547 participants in the U.S. All of Us Research Program. Age-specific onset rates for 274 high-burden diseases between ages 21 and 74 were analyzed. Standardized onset curves were grouped using hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Aging-related patterns were assessed with Gompertz and Gompertz-Makeham (GM) models to quantify age-dependent increases in disease onset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eleven clusters of disease onset trajectories were identified, with four main clusters encompassing 96.0% of diseases. Two clusters exhibited pronounced late-life increases in onset rate, while one showed earlier but moderate age-related increases, and another displayed largely age-independent patterns. Cardiovascular diseases and cancers were enriched in clusters with strong aging-related onset trajectories. Overall, 165 diseases demonstrated strong evidence of being aging-related, characterized by positive Gompertz age coefficients and good GM model fit. Median onset ages varied across clusters and disease categories and showed statistically significant discrepancies compared with U.K. populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a large, racially diverse U.S. cohort, we identified distinct ARD clusters with shared age-related onset patterns. These findings extend prior work to a more diverse population and support integrated clustering and actuarial approaches to systematically define ARDs and inform aging research and public health strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Aging-Related Diseases in the U.S. Population: A Data-Driven Approach Using All of Us Electronic Health Record Data

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive reserve (CR) is thought to buffer against the clinical manifestation of dementia, preserving cognitive function despite accumulating pathology. However, less is known about how CR relates to the capacity to independently perform activities of daily living (ADL), particularly among cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults. Here, we investigated this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline data from 1,571 CU participants (mean age: 64.7±7.6; 81.3% female) from the CAN-PROTECT study were analyzed. A composite CR score was derived from education, occupational complexity, and engagement in cognitively stimulating activities. Functional ability was measured using the Standard Assessment of Global Everyday Activities (SAGEA) scale, capturing cognitive, applied cognitive, instrumental, and basic ADL, and mobility. Negative binomial models examined associations between CR and global and domain-specific ADL, adjusting for age, sex, cognition, behaviour, and physical/sensory limitations. Additional models tested the independent contribution of CR components to functional outcomes. Mediation analyses assessed the effect of CR on quality of life (QoL) through ADL abilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher CR was associated with lower global ADL impairment (count ratio=0.58, 95%CI: 0.36-0.94, p = 0.027), driven by 49% less impairment in applied cognitive ADL (95%CI: 0.26-0.97, p = 0.038). Among CR domains, education showed the most consistent association with lower impairment across all ADL domains and was indirectly linked to better QoL through improved function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CR, particularly education, may play an important role in supporting functional abilities and QoL among CU older adults. Enhancing CR may be a promising avenue to promote functional independence and healthy aging, even in the absence of cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Brain aging characterized by progressive structural and functional changes, including atrophy of the hippocampus and frontal cortex, reduced neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, and disruptions in network connectivity, collectively impairing memory, attention, and executive functions. However, aging is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous process, with variability in decline and preservation of certain cognitive capacities supported by compensatory mechanisms. Neuroplasticity plays a central role in mitigating age-related losses by enabling functional reorganization and maintaining neural connectivity. This integrative review synthesizes evidence on the effects of physical activity, sensory stimulation, and multisystem interventions on brain aging. Aerobic and multicomponent exercise programs, particularly those lasting 8–24 weeks, have been associated with improvements in hippocampal volume, executive function, and mobility. These benefits appear to be mediated by upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, lactate signaling, and cathepsin B, which support synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and cerebral perfusion. Sensory stimulation enhances neural processing through multisensory integration, strengthening connectivity within attentional and executive networks. Combined interventions that integrate motor, sensory, and cognitive components appear promising and may offer advantages over single‑domain approaches, although direct comparative evidence remains limited. Activities such as dance, proprioceptive training, and musical engagement exemplify sensorimotor integration, promoting cognitive reserve. In addition, emerging technologies, including virtual reality and brain-computer interfaces, further support personalized, neuroplasticity-driven rehabilitation. Together, these findings highlight sensorimotor integration as a central mechanism for preserving cognitive and functional capacity and promoting healthy brain aging.</jats:p>
title: The effects of physical and sensory activities on motor and cognitive functions in the aging brain: a review

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More than one-in-five older adults live in the rural U.S. Adults living in rural U.S. experience significantly higher hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular disease-related mortality compared to their urban counterparts. To extend the literature and provide real-world evidence, the primary objective of this study was to estimate the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension and to identify factors associated with it among Medicare beneficiaries receiving care in rural South Carolina.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were used from the annual review of Abbeville County Medicare patients diagnosed with hypertension between July 2024 and January 2025. Uncontrolled hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg with or without antihypertensive medications. Generalized linear models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used to examine individual, behavioral, clinical, and area-level contextual factors associated with uncontrolled hypertension.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Responses from 813 Medicare beneficiaries with diagnosed hypertension were analyzed: 55.6% females with a mean age (standard deviation) of 73.2±8.48 years. Overall, the prevalence (95% CI) of uncontrolled hypertension was 76.3% (95% CI: 73.2, 79.1). Compared with a healthy weight, being overweight (aOR=2.0; 95% CI: 1.2, 3.3; p =  0.005) or obese (aOR=2.1; 95% CI: 1.1, 2.8; p = 0.010) was associated with higher odds of uncontrolled hypertension. Contrary to previous findings, “most of the time” PA (aOR=1.57; 95% CI: 1.05-2.34; p = 0.027) was associated with a higher likelihood of uncontrolled hypertension compared to no PA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings highlight a high burden of uncontrolled hypertension in a rural Medicare population, underscore the need for objective measures and further studies into the individual, behavioral, clinical, and contextual factors that may contribute to blood pressure control in rural communities.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>The patterns and determinants of late-life functional decline are not fully understood.                   <jats:p>Statins have pleiotropic properties beyond LDL cholesterol reduction, including anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects that may influence biological aging and frailty. Secondary objectives included differences in walking speed, short physical performance battery, and hand grip strength. Baseline was the first visit with a FI assessment; follow-up was the last visit. Statin users and non-users were matched for follow-up duration. Time 0 (T0) was defined as statin initiation. Frailty was assessed with a 34-item FI. To minimize collider bias, lipid variables were excluded from the FI due to their direct relationship with statin exposure. Frailty trajectories and secondary outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed models. Beta-estimates were multiplied by 100 to improve readability. Among 3,444 people with HIV (69% men; median age 44.7 years), 23.1% initiated statins for primary prevention and 2.0% for secondary prevention. Statin users had a more unfavorable cardiometabolic profile at T0. In adjusted models, statin use was associated with a reduction in FI over time (statin*time interaction β=–2.562, 95%-CI –3.176,–1.987). No associations were observed with secondary outcomes. Statins may improve frailty trajectories, mitigate aging-related decline and preserve physical function in people with HIV, supporting a broader role for statins in HIV care.</jats:p>
